title: Before You Hand Your Wallet to AI, the Payment Network Has to Be Rewritten
dek: Only one of the four guests had actually paid for something with an Agent — 40-odd yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology, it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely believe in an intelligent agent.
why: A live roundtable at the Bund Summit, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is medium, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth listening to.
who: Founders and product leads working on payments, Agent products and AI infrastructure — especially those designing authorization, identity and transaction flows.
skip: 28:44 to 30:36, on how large models pick a coffee shop. It's basically a recap of the search-and-recommendation process, with no new information.

points.h: Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg loop
points.body: Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but actual deployment this year has been much slower than expected. From conversations with merchants he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good Agent services; merchants see no users using it, so they dare not invest in development. His solution is for Ant to act as a catalyst — using the analogy from the chemistry he learned as a child, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. The concrete move is the ‘wishing wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an Agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, useful Agents, so the flywheel starts turning.

points.h: Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
points.body: Jorn Lambert said all of today's systems are designed on the assumption that a human is involved — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they have to be redesigned. He broke it into three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else operating your account; second, confirming that the entity executing the task is a real, trusted agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction has to be clear enough — he said ‘tomorrow evening’ is not clear whether it means 6 or 9, so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the moment of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the whole transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant made an error, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

points.h: What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
points.body: Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following has improved substantially over the past few years and is getting stronger, but in practice models often feel like they don't understand the individual well enough, mainly because of missing context — a person's understanding of something comes from long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models don't have, and an Agent System needs to organize the relevant information effectively. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models need to learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; people ask when they're unsure, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when unsure — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. On task execution, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, traceability and auditability, and that these don't come entirely from the model — the model and the Agent Harness need to jointly create the environment.

points.h: KYA is the new link after KYC
points.body: Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, Agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On identity, he specifically noted that beyond the original KYC and KYB, there also needs to be Know Your Agent, i.e. KYA. On capability assessment, he said plainly that very little is being done today — why should I trust that a merchant's Agent can satisfy my needs well. The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong, the system can automatically determine who made the mistake: the user authorized wrongly, their own Agent didn't understand clearly, information was passed incorrectly, or the merchant's Agent executed poorly. Finally he cautioned that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people were relatively accepting.

points.h: The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's the consumer
points.body: Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very nerve-wracking, and now nobody worries, because over the years consumers were shown there would be protection, with recourse and remedies when things go wrong. He said we now need to prove it again, and are putting the standards up piece by piece — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Two things next: getting thousands of companies worldwide to connect to this system, and getting consumers to believe the mechanism actually works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck is not technology but ordinary consumers, who need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there is a lot to learn from China.

points.h: The Pilates class test exposes a permissions problem
points.body: Hong Jun gave an example: asking the model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the Agent found that time slot was fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the users ahead and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks you've authorized the Agent to do — you asked it to book an appointment, but does it also have permission to delete other people. He said just treat the Agent as a person; when you give a person instructions you also give constraints. What the model side needs to do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while handling the task — it shouldn't, just because it read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan, drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A and it going off to do B.

points.h: Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
points.body: Han Xinyi laid out the new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifting from time spent to intent; the path of the personal assistant is getting clearer, and he summarized several consensus features: personalized, somewhat proactive, full-modality interaction, long time series, and not just on phones — many startups are doing it in the form of applications too. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to raise conversion rates, to solving problems based on the user's individual intent, more precisely. On the supply side, paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and cannot be generalized or replicated, and AI large models can expand that supply. He ended with a neuron analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, assume 10 Agents each, that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections; if the Agents in today's economy reach the same scale and connection depth, the generalization would bring enormous business opportunities.

points.h: Agents have no bank card, credentials must be rebuilt
points.body: Jorn Lambert said an agent today has no bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay; it needs a completely different kind of credential, and that credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to businesses, and businesses need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged this system will very likely be built on blockchain, and must be as fast as machines, with massive microtransactions completed in the blink of an eye, requiring completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build such infrastructure; as for innovators, they will create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will look like, and rather than trying to predict the future, it's better to lay the tracks first.

terms.def: Know Your Agent, an additional layer of identity verification beyond KYC and KYB, confirming that the entity executing the task is a trusted agent.
A commercial form in which AI agents complete discovery, ordering, payment and other transaction steps on behalf of people.
A layer of system wrapped around the model, responsible for permission control, authorization, traceability and a secure execution environment.
Agent to Agent, referring to autonomous interaction and transactions between agents, requiring a set of protocols similar to social norms.
The word Jorn Lambert uses to describe the explosive entrepreneurial growth brought by the development of agents.
